terms.brief: The Python/PyTorch environment the app needs to run
terms.detail: The Python environment the engine depends on (PyTorch, etc.). Not included in the installer; the right version is downloaded automatically for your GPU on first launch.

terms.brief: Base model that turns audio into content features (shared by all voices)
terms.detail: Hubert extracts "what was said" from your speech and passes it to the voice model. It's shared by every voice — one file for the whole app, and no voice works without it.

terms.brief: Pre-trained model you start from when training a custom voice
terms.detail: Officially pre-trained general acoustic models. Training from one is much faster than from scratch. They come in 32k / 40k / 48k; download the one matching your sample rate first.

terms.brief: The .index feature file that comes with a voice, for better fidelity
terms.detail: The index stores features of the training audio. With it, the output is closer to the original voice, though articulation may soften. Optional — conversion works without it. Strength is set under "Index strength" in Settings.

terms.brief: GPU acceleration for AMD / integrated graphics; converts voice but can't train
terms.detail: DirectML is Windows' GPU acceleration for non-NVIDIA cards (AMD, Intel integrated). It lacks some operators training needs, so training still requires an NVIDIA card.

terms.brief: Inference speed-up for NVIDIA cards; falls back automatically if unsupported
terms.detail: Pre-records GPU inference commands to cut CPU–GPU overhead, lowering latency and VRAM use. NVIDIA only; falls back to the normal mode automatically if incompatible.

terms.brief: rmvpe / harvest / pm / fcpe / crepe; RMVPE is the usual choice
terms.detail: Determines how the app detects the pitch of your voice. RMVPE is the best and fastest — leave it. Harvest is steadier but slower; PM is fastest but prone to cracking; FCPE and Crepe are optional high-accuracy options.

terms.brief: Controls how thick or thin the voice sounds; labeled "Formant" in the UI
terms.detail: Formants decide whether a voice sounds thick or thin. Fine-tune it alongside pitch, without changing pitch itself, to get closer to the target character.

terms.brief: Input noise gate: quieter sounds count as silence
terms.detail: Sounds below this level (keyboard, fans, etc.) are treated as silence and not converted. When you speak, the level bar should clearly cross the line — otherwise it's set too high.

terms.brief: Whether output volume follows your original voice or the target voice
terms.detail: How much output volume follows your original voice: lower stays closer to the trained voice's own loudness, higher keeps your natural dynamics.

terms.brief: How audio blocks are joined; more natural on some voices
terms.detail: Joins adjacent audio blocks differently. Smoother on some voices, no difference on others — A/B it to decide.

terms.brief: Audio samples per second (usually 32k / 40k / 48k)
terms.detail: Samples per second, usually 32k / 40k / 48k. Follow the sound card or the voice model — if unsure, keep "Follow device".

terms.brief: Windows' classic audio API, best compatibility
terms.detail: The oldest Windows audio API: best compatibility, works with almost any device, at the cost of higher latency. Pick it if unsure. Restart the voice changer after changing.

terms.brief: Lower latency than MME, but pickier about devices
terms.detail: Newer than MME with much lower latency — good when response time matters. Pickier about devices and drivers, though; some sound cards go silent or error out, and switching back to MME fixes it. Its "Exclusive" mode lowers latency further but locks the whole card.

terms.brief: Low-latency interface for pro sound cards; only appears once the driver is installed
terms.detail: Provided by pro recording cards and drivers like ASIO4ALL — the lowest latency of all. It only shows up after the driver is installed; if it's absent, the device doesn't support it. Only one program can use it at a time.

terms.brief: Lets you hear your own converted voice
terms.detail: By default the converted voice only goes to games/voice chat. Monitor sends a copy to your headphones too. Pick real headphones or speakers as the monitor device — a virtual card gives you silence and possible feedback.

terms.brief: How much audio is processed at once: shorter means faster but heavier
terms.detail: The app cuts audio into small blocks and processes them in real time. Smaller blocks mean lower latency but more GPU load; too small and audio stutters. Restart the voice changer after changing.

terms.brief: Transition length at the seams between audio blocks
terms.detail: Adjacent blocks overlap slightly so seams don't click. Too short clicks, too long smears. The default is fine.

terms.brief: Smooths out volume swings
terms.detail: When your voice jumps in volume, the compressor tames the loud parts for a steadier sound. More compression is flatter, but too much sounds dull and lifeless.

terms.brief: Adjusts brightness and body of the voice by frequency band
terms.detail: Splits the sound into high/mid/low bands and adjusts each. Muffled? Boost the highs. Thin? Boost the lows. Not sure? Start with a preset.

terms.brief: A virtual audio cable between the app and your games (VB-Cable)
terms.detail: It's a wire inside your PC: the app sends converted audio to CABLE Input, you set the game's mic to CABLE Output, and everyone hears you. Restart the PC after installing, or the two devices won't show up.

terms.brief: The voice-conversion tech this app is built on
terms.detail: RVC (Retrieval-based Voice Conversion): each voice is a standalone model, and switching voices means switching model files.

s.inferGuideLead: Pick a vocal clip and convert it to the selected voice. Use defaults if unsure.
s.inferGuideQ1: How is this different from live conversion?
s.inferGuideA1: Convert existing audio files to the target voice. Real-time voice change is on the main page; both share voice and engine resources (hubert / rmvpe).
s.inferGuideA2: rmvpe works best, harvest is stable but slow for low pitch, pm is fast but may crack, crepe is good but uses more VRAM. Offline conversion has no fcpe.
s.inferGuideQ3: What are protect and the volume envelope?
s.inferGuideA3: Protect stops consonants and breath from tearing; 0.5 disables it. Envelope near 0 follows source loudness. Filter radius only matters for harvest. Resample 0 keeps the rate.
s.inferGuideQ4: How do I batch, and which format?
s.inferGuideA4: A folder is scanned recursively and the output keeps the same subfolders. One bad file is skipped. Download the engine pack first if it is missing. Formats: wav / flac / mp3 / m4a.
s.sepGuideLead: Extract vocals or accompaniment from songs. Separation is powered by PyMSS; models download on demand.
s.sepGuideH1: Vocal extract first; de-echo / de-reverb as needed
s.sepGuideA1: For training prep, download 'Vocal Extraction'. For lead vocal isolation, use 'Karaoke'. De-echo and de-reverb as needed. HP2 is heavier; not needed for daily use.
s.sepGuideQ2: Can I process a whole folder?
s.sepGuideA2: Supports batch folder processing: one file or a folder. Only one job at a time so two runs do not fight over VRAM.
s.sepGuideA3: 0–20. Higher is cleaner and more likely to thin the vocal. Leave 10 if unsure. Export as wav / flac / mp3 / m4a.
s.sepGuideA4: Separation engine is PyMSS. For stereo de-reverb, download 'De-reverb' from the Plaza; for de-echo, download 'De-echo'. Recommended flow: vocal extraction first, then de-echo/de-reverb as needed.

s.trainGuideLead: Train your own voice from clean dry vocal material. Use defaults if unsure.
s.trainGuideH1: NVIDIA GPU, base models, clean vocals
s.trainGuideA1: You need an NVIDIA GPU, a finished Runtime install, the pretrained models for your sample rate, and clean dry vocals — no backing track, no second speaker. Run Vocal Separate on songs first. Aim for 10+ minutes; a tiny set overfits and only sings those few lines.
s.trainGuideQ2: How should I lay out the files, and which sample rate?
s.trainGuideA2: Put the dry vocals in one folder; nested folders are scanned too. Keep one speaker, one style, one recording chain. Don't clip, don't add reverb. 48k has the most detail and uses the most VRAM; 40k is the usual community trade-off; 32k is lightest. Download the matching pretrained pack. Resume keeps the sample rate of the slices you already have.
s.trainGuideH3: Start around 200 for clean audio, then listen
s.trainGuideA3: One epoch is one full pass over the slices. Clean audio is often worth 150–300 before you listen; noisier audio often sounds better with fewer (tens to about 100) than with too many. Default 20 is a sample value. For home use, start from 200, listen, then continue if needed.
s.trainGuideQ4: What is batch size? Why do I run out of VRAM?
s.trainGuideH4: Slices per step; about VRAM GB ÷ 2
s.trainGuideA4: Batch size is how many slices the GPU sees at once. Generally, VRAM GB divided by 2 (6GB ≈ 3, 8GB ≈ 4). Larger is stabler and faster until you OOM. If you OOM, lower the batch and resume with the same name — the slices stay.
s.trainGuideH5: Use rmvpe unless you have a reason
s.trainGuideA5: This is how pitch is read during training. rmvpe is usually best. harvest is slower and more stable on noisy audio. pm is fastest but cracks easily. Pick well at train time; you can use a different algorithm later for live conversion.
s.trainGuideQ6: Where is the model? What if I close the app?
s.trainGuideH6: It shows up under Models; same name resumes
s.trainGuideA6: When training finishes the voice appears on the Models page, and the .pth is also under assets/weights. If you quit mid-run, use the same name next time to skip finished steps. Checkpoints keep only the latest large weights; turn on “save a usable model” to write a listen-ready file every N epochs. An index is optional but closer to the original voice.

s.dspTipFxPitch: Raises or lowers pitch without changing how thick the voice is. Up is chipmunk, down is giant.
s.dspTipFxFormant: Moves resonance only. Up is thinner, down is thicker. Opposite of pitch is a gender swap.
s.dspTipFxWhisper: Breaks up harmonics so it sounds breathy.
s.dspTipFxRobot: Drives a pulse carrier with your speech envelope — cheap vocoder metal you can still talk through.
s.dspTipFxRing: Modulates the voice with a tone — metallic or robotic.
s.dspTipFxTremolo: Volume wobble. Alien and radio use this.
s.dspTipFxChorus: Stacks slightly detuned copies so it sounds like more than one person.
s.dspTipFxBitcrush: Drops bit depth and sample rate — old game-console grit.
s.dspTipFxRadio: Cuts highs and lows, optional hiss. Walkie-talkie, phone, old radio.
s.dspTipFxReverb: Space / room. Cave or empty hall.
s.dspTipPSemitones: How many semitones to shift pitch. +12 is an octave up, -12 an octave down. Thickness stays put.
s.dspTipPShift: How many semitones to move resonance. Up is thinner, down is thicker. Pitch stays put.
s.dspTipPAmount: How strong this effect is. 0 is almost off; all the way up is maximum.
s.dspTipPFreq: Modulation frequency in hertz. Lower is heavier metal; higher is thinner and more electronic.
s.dspTipPMix: Dry vs wet. 0 is the original voice; 1 is all effect.
s.dspTipPRate: How fast the wobble or sweep is. Higher means denser motion.
s.dspTipPDepth: How far the wobble or sweep goes. Higher means a bigger swing.
s.dspTipPVoices: How many slightly detuned copies. 2 is a pair; 3 sounds more like a crowd.
s.dspTipPBits: Bits per sample. 16 is normal; lower gets crunchier and more digital.
s.dspTipPDownsample: How hard to thin the sample rate. 1 is none; higher is muddier, like an old console.
s.dspTipPLow: Lowest frequency kept. Push it up to cut more bass and thin the voice.
s.dspTipPHigh: Highest frequency kept. Pull it down to cut more treble and dull the voice.
s.dspTipPNoise: How much hiss. 0 is clean; higher sounds like a badly tuned station.
s.dspTipPTimeMs: Echo delay in milliseconds. Short is a small room; long is a valley.
s.dspTipPFeedback: How much echo is fed back. Higher means more repeats; too high can ring.
s.dspTipPSize: How big the space is. Small is a room; large is a cave or hall.

s.outGainTip: Sets how loud the converted voice is sent out. Raise it if others hear you too quietly. Too much clips and distorts — keep the output meter off the top.
s.mainGpuTip:
Selects which NVIDIA GPU performs the computation when more than one is present.
The engine defaults to the lowest-numbered device. On a machine with both a 5060 and a 5090, that default is frequently not the faster card.
Changes take effect the next time voice conversion is started.
If conversion fails to start after changing this, or reports insufficient VRAM, revert to “Automatic” first: when the selected index does not correspond to a device the driver actually enumerates, the engine falls back to a slower backend because it can find no GPU at all.
This setting has no effect on AMD or integrated graphics (DirectML).
s.computeBackendTip:
The device the engine is currently computing on.
The backend is selected automatically: CUDA is preferred, falling back to DirectML and then CPU. A fallback raises latency substantially, and on some machines also reports insufficient VRAM because a virtual display adapter was selected.
If the result shown here is not what you expect, review the “Primary GPU” setting and your display driver.
s.computeBackendWarn: The NVIDIA runtime is installed, but CUDA is not in use. Revert “Primary GPU” to “Automatic”, or update your NVIDIA driver and try again.
s.firstRunLead: Seven steps from a fresh install to the other side hearing you. If you only want to hear it yourself, stop at step five.
s.firstRunH1: Prompted on first launch · roughly 2–4 GB
s.firstRunA1:
Voice-model conversion needs its own runtime environment. The app asks on first launch and downloads it for you — pick the build that matches your graphics card.
You can skip this if you only want DSP voice: those twenty built-in presets need no runtime.
Once it is installed, Other → Run status shows it as ready.
s.firstRunH2: You must restart the computer afterwards
s.firstRunA2:
For people in a game or voice app to hear the converted voice, a virtual audio device has to carry it there. You can install VB-Cable at the top of this page.
Restart the computer after installing, or CABLE Input and CABLE Output will not appear in the device list. Signing out or restarting the app is not enough.
If you already have a virtual audio device such as VoiceMeeter, do not install another one — a second set only adds devices that are easy to wire up wrong.
s.firstRunH3: Download one from the Plaza, or use a DSP preset
s.firstRunA3:
The Plaza page downloads ready-made voices directly; they then appear on the Models page and on the main screen.
For a .pth file someone sent you, import it on the Models page.
If you would rather not download a model, DSP voice on the main screen has twenty built-in presets — pick one and you have sound, on any graphics card.
s.firstRunH4: Input is your real microphone, output is CABLE Input
s.firstRunA4:
Under Settings → Device & Audio, set the input device to your real microphone and the output device to CABLE Input.
To hear your own converted voice at the same time, tick “Monitor myself” and set the monitor device to real headphones — not CABLE.
Leave the Windows default playback device on your headphones or speakers. Do not change it to CABLE, or you will hear nothing at all yourself.
s.firstRunA5:
Go back to the main screen, pick a voice and press Start. The first run loads the runtime and the model, usually 20–40 seconds; later runs are much faster.
Speak into the microphone and the input level in the bottom bar moves — if it moves, the microphone is getting through.
If you ticked monitoring, this is when you hear your converted self in the headphones.
s.firstRunQ6: 6. Let the other side hear it
s.firstRunH6: Set the other app's microphone to CABLE Output
s.firstRunA6:
In the game or voice app's own settings, change the microphone (input device) to CABLE Output. This cannot be done from here — it has to be done in that application.
Discord: Settings → Voice & Video → Input Device.
OBS: the Audio Input Capture source → Device.
Zoom / Teams: Settings → Audio → Microphone.
Games usually keep it under Audio or Voice in their settings.
Afterwards, use that app's own microphone test to listen — if you hear the converted voice, it is working.
s.firstRunH7: Three checks; whichever one fails tells you where to look
s.firstRunA7:
① The input level in the bottom bar moves while you speak — the microphone is getting in. If it does not move, check the input device and the response threshold.
② With “Monitor myself” ticked, you hear the converted voice in your headphones — the engine is working. If you do not, check the monitor device and the selected voice.
③ The other side, or that app's own microphone test, hears it — the routing works. If not, check whether that app's microphone is set to CABLE Output.
Whichever of the three fails, look up the matching entry under Common issues below.
s.faqVoiceUnlikeQ: The result does not sound like the voice — robotic or glitchy
s.faqVoiceUnlikeH: Get the pitch right first, then raise the index strength
s.faqVoiceUnlikeA:
Nine times out of ten the pitch is wrong. A male voice using a female model wants Pitch at +12; a female voice using a male model, −12; between the same gender, leave it at 0.
An octave off sounds either strained or heavily robotic. That is not the model's fault.
If the pitch is right and it still does not match, raise the index strength — start around 0.75. It controls how closely the output follows the training material. At 1 it sometimes drags the source noise floor along with it.
Formant controls how thin or thick the voice is: negative is thinner, positive is thicker. Move it 0.1 at a time.
Leave the pitch algorithm on rmvpe; it is the most accurate.
s.faqNoCableQ: The virtual audio device is installed but CABLE is not in the device list
s.faqNoCableH: VB-Cable needs a full restart after installing
s.faqNoCableA:
VB-Cable is a system-level driver. The computer has to be restarted before it appears in the device list — signing out or restarting the app is not enough.
If it is still missing after a restart, press “Reload device list” under Settings → Device & Audio.
If it is still missing, install it again. Windows shows an administrator prompt during installation and you have to accept it; declining leaves it uninstalled without necessarily reporting an error.
s.faqSelfSilentQ: After starting conversion I cannot hear anything at all
s.faqSelfSilentH: Do not set the Windows default playback device to CABLE
s.faqSelfSilentA:
Setting the output device to CABLE Input sends your voice to the other side. It is not what you listen through.
If the Windows default playback device is also set to CABLE, every sound on the system is fed into the virtual cable and of course you hear nothing. Keep Windows default playback on your headphones or speakers.
To hear your own converted voice, tick “Monitor myself” under Settings → Device & Audio and set the monitor device to real headphones.
s.faqEchoQ: I hear an echo, or my voice doubled
s.faqEchoH: Keep the monitor device off CABLE, and turn off microphone playback
s.faqEchoA:
If the monitor device is set to one of the CABLE devices, the sound loops back on itself — that is what the echo, or the squeal, is. The monitor device has to be real headphones or speakers.
If the voice app also has a microphone test or playback running, that adds a second layer. Turn it off.
Speakers cause echo far more easily than headphones, because the sound leaves the speaker and goes straight back into the microphone. Prefer headphones.
s.faqThresholdQ: Nothing happens when I speak, or I have to shout
s.faqThresholdH: Adjust Settings → Device & Audio → Response threshold
s.faqThresholdA:
The response threshold decides how loud a sound has to be before it counts as speech and gets converted. Too high and normal speech is discarded as noise; too low and keystrokes and fan noise get converted too.
Start at −60 dB and move it 5 at a time. The level bar in the bottom bar shows the current volume against the threshold line — adjusting against that is the fastest way.
If the microphone itself is quiet, raise the mic gain rather than pushing the threshold ever lower; lowering it just lets the noise floor in.
s.faqLoudnessQ: The other side says it is too quiet, or that it clips
s.faqLoudnessH: Adjust the output volume, and back off if it distorts
s.faqLoudnessA:
Settings → Device & Audio → Output volume (dB) sets the overall level sent to the other side. Raise it if it is too quiet.
Too far and it clips and distorts. Judge it by keeping the output level in the bottom bar off the ceiling.
If the input is already quiet, raise the mic gain first. If both are maxed and it is still not enough, check the microphone's own level and boost in the Windows sound settings.
s.faqGpuNeedQ: Do I need an NVIDIA card? Do AMD and integrated graphics work?
s.faqGpuNeedH: DSP works on anything; voice conversion runs on AMD too, just slower
s.faqGpuNeedA:
The twenty DSP presets run purely on the CPU. They work on any machine, with no runtime and no model to download.
Voice-model conversion (RVC) is fastest on NVIDIA. AMD and integrated graphics go through DirectML — it works, but latency is higher and the block size has to be raised for it to stay stable.
On a machine with integrated graphics only, try DSP voice first to get a feel for it.
Other → Run status → Compute backend shows what the engine is actually using.
s.faqVramQ: It says there is not enough VRAM and will not start
s.faqVramH: Set Other → Primary GPU back to Automatic
s.faqVramA:
On a multi-GPU machine, if the index selected under Primary GPU does not match what the display driver actually enumerates, the engine finds no GPU at all and falls back to a virtual display adapter — which surfaces as insufficient VRAM.
Set Other → Run status → Primary GPU back to “Auto (unspecified)”, then start conversion again.
Compute backend, in the same group, shows what the engine is really using. It has to read CUDA for an NVIDIA card to be doing the work.
If Automatic still does not help, update your NVIDIA driver and try again.
s.faqAlreadyRunningH: It is probably already running, in the background or the tray
s.faqAlreadyRunningA:
Only one copy of this app can run at a time. Clicking the icon while it is already running brings the existing window to the front instead of opening a second one — two engines would fight over the same graphics card and the same microphone.
The window may be minimised to the tray; check the icons at the right of the taskbar.
Settings → General → On window close decides whether the X minimises to tray or quits outright.
s.faqAntivirusQ: Antivirus flags it, or Windows blocks the install
s.faqAntivirusH: Add the whole install folder to the trusted list
s.faqAntivirusA:
The app ships a complete Python runtime and unpacks and runs a great many scripts, which some antivirus products flag on behaviour alone.
When Windows says it protected your PC, choose More info → Run anyway.
For antivirus, add the entire install folder to the trusted list and install again. Allowing only the main executable is not enough — what gets removed is usually a file inside the runtime, and the symptom is an install that finishes but whose engine will not start.
s.faqDownloadSlowQ: The runtime download is slow or keeps stopping
s.faqDownloadSlowH: Retrying resumes; it does not start over
s.faqDownloadSlowA:
Pressing it again after a failure resumes from where it stopped. What already downloaded is not fetched twice.
If the progress sits still for a long time, first check that the network can reach the internet at all.
If it will not download at all, ask the community for an offline package via Other → Repository & social.
s.faqLatencyQ: Why is there a delay, and can it be shorter?
s.faqLatencyH: Around three hundred milliseconds is normal
s.faqLatencyA:
Latency = block size + crossfade + the sound card's own delay. At the default settings that is a little over three hundred milliseconds. It is inherent to real-time conversion, not a fault.
To lower it, reduce Settings → Performance → Block size. The cost is more load on the graphics card and a greater chance of dropouts.
Performance settings only take effect after starting conversion again.
s.faqBypassQ: I want my own voice back for a moment, or a different voice mid-session
s.faqBypassH: The Converted / Original toggle; switching voices needs no restart
s.faqBypassA:
Converted / Original in the bottom bar switches straight back to your own voice without stopping the engine.
Settings → Hotkeys can bind a key to it; tick “Global” and it works from inside a game too.
Switching voices needs no restart either: while it is running, just pick another voice on the main screen and it changes seamlessly.
s.faqOfflineQ: I just want to convert a recording, not talk in a game
s.faqOfflineH: Use Voice conversion — no virtual audio device needed
s.faqOfflineA:
Audio tools → Voice conversion, below the main screen: pick an audio file or a whole folder, convert it to the current voice and export.
This route needs no virtual audio device and no real-time conversion.
To pull the vocals out of a song first, use Vocal separation next to it.

extras.engineDesc: hubert / rmvpe / ffmpeg. Required for real-time VC, speech conversion, and training. First setup only downloads Runtime; get this when you need it.

pymss-vocal.label: Vocal extraction
pymss-vocal.notes: Top choice for cleaning training material — extracts dry vocals from songs.

pymss-denoise.label: Denoise
pymss-denoise.notes: Removes background noise and hum. Download when dry vocals are noisy.

pymss-deecho.label: De-echo
pymss-deecho.notes: Removes room echo / delay tails. Useful in spacious recording environments.

pymss-inst.label: Instrumental extract
pymss-inst.notes: Extracts the accompaniment track (opposite of vocal extraction).

pymss-karaoke.label: Karaoke (remove vocal)
pymss-karaoke.notes: Removes lead vocals to create backing tracks.

pymss-bve.label: Background vocals (advanced)
pymss-bve.notes: Separate background harmony tracks. Rarely needed for training material.

pymss-harmonic.label: Harmonic/noise (advanced)
pymss-harmonic.notes: Separate harmonics and noise. Advanced use.

pymss-hp2.label: HP2 high quality (advanced)
pymss-hp2.notes: Heavier HP2 series, higher quality, larger (~1.5GB). Daily use: Vocal extraction is enough.

pymss-mgm.label: MGM fusion (advanced)
pymss-mgm.notes: MGM v4 multi-band fusion model. Advanced use.

pymss-sp.label: SP spectrum series (advanced)
pymss-sp.notes: SP spectral series. Large download; only needed for special cases.

pretrained-v2-32k.label: Base model 32k
pretrained-v2-32k.notes: Needed to train 32k voices. Less VRAM; slightly lower quality than 48k.

pretrained-v2-40k.label: Base model 40k
pretrained-v2-40k.notes: Needed to train 40k voices. Pick one of 32k/40k/48k — no need for all.

pretrained-v2-48k.label: Base model 48k
pretrained-v2-48k.notes: For training custom voices. Download only the sample rate you use; 48k is best quality, more VRAM. Includes G/D/f0G/f0D like RVC pretrained_v2.
